claim: Roughly a third of datasets in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) come from experiments profiling dynamic processes over time.
source: Indeed, analysis of the largest repository of gene expression experiments, the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), determined that roughly a third of these datasets come from experiments profiling dynamic processes over time (Zinman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zinman et al., 2013, which analyzed the GEO repository.

claim: miRNAs have been known to regulate lung development.
source: miRNAs have been known to regulate lung development (Sessa and Hata, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sessa and Hata, 2013.

claim: Several miRNAs are differentially expressed during lung developmental process.
source: several miRNAs are differentially expressed during this developmental process (Williams et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2007.

claim: Several miRNAs are coordinately activated with various TFs to control specific transitions during development.
source: Several of these are also coordinately activated with various TFs to control specific transitions during development (Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schulz et al., 2013.

claim: TPS utilizes expression data from a small set of genes sampled at a high rate.
source: TPS utilizes expression data from a small set of genes sampled at a high rate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the TPS method.

claim: The points selected by TPS can be used to reconstruct an accurate representation for the expression values of the non selected points.
source: As we show by applying TPS to study mouse lung development, the points selected by TPS can be used to reconstruct an accurate representation for the expression values of the non selected points.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Even though the selection is only based on gene expression, these points are also appropriate for representing a much larger set of protein, miRNA and DNA methylation changes over time.
source: Further, even though the selection is only based on gene expression, these points are also appropriate for representing a much larger set of protein, miRNA and DNA methylation changes over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5, showing miRNA and DNA methylation results.

claim: A total of 240 samples were isolated by Laser Capture Microscopy (LCM) from murine lung at multiple time points.
source: A total of 240 samples were isolated by Laser Capture Microscopy (LCM) from murine lung at multiple time points (E16.5, P.05 to P14 every 12 hr, and P15 to P28 every 24 hr).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: 126 genes known or suspected to be involved in lung development were profiled using NanoString.
source: We first profiled the expression of 126 genes known or suspected to be involved in lung development using NanoString (See Appendix Methods for a list of the selected genes and the reason each was selected).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and data collection.

claim: TPS shows significant performance improvement when compared to randomly selected points.
source: As expected, we find significant performance improvement when using TPS when compared to randomly selected points.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2, which compares TPS to random selection.

claim: TPS shows significant and consistent improvement over uniform sampling for all sizes of selected time points.
source: Importantly, we also see a significant and consistent improvement (for all sizes of selected time points) over uniform sampling highlighting the advantage of condition-specific sampling decisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2, which compares TPS to uniform sampling across different numbers of selected points.

claim: As the number of points used by TPS increases, it leads to results that are very close to the error represented by noise in the data (0.108).
source: As the number of points used by TPS increases, it leads to results that are very close to the error represented by noise in the data (0.108) ( Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with a specific noise value of 0.108.

claim: When using the points selected based on the mRNA data, a much lower error is achieved when compared to the error resulting from using the same number of uniform or random points (p<0.01 for random based on randomization analysis).
source: As can be seen, when using the points selected based on the mRNA data we achieve a much lower error when compared to the error resulting from using the same number of uniform or random points (p<0.01 for random based on randomization analysis)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (p<0.01) and data presented in Figure 4.

claim: When using the 13 selected mRNA points, the average mean squared error is 0.4312 whereas when using the optimal points based on the miRNA data itself the error is 0.4042.
source: For example, when using the 13 selected mRNA points, the average mean squared error is 0.4312 whereas when using the optimal points based on the miRNA data itself the error is 0.4042.
evidence: This claim provides specific numerical values for reconstruction errors under different conditions.

claim: The 4 points identified using the mRNA data (0.5, 5, 15, 26) were exactly the same as the ones selected using the methylation data.
source: The 4 points identified using the mRNA data (0.5, 5, 15, 26) were exactly the same as the ones selected using the methylation data indicating again that mRNA data is a good proxy for the dynamics of the epigenetic data as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct comparison of time points selected by different methods.

claim: TPS utilizes splines to represent temporal profiles and implements a cross-validation strategy to evaluate potential sets of points.
source: TPS utilizes splines to represent temporal profiles and implements a cross-validation strategy to evaluate potential sets of points.
evidence: This is a description of the TPS methodology.

claim: TPS employs a greedy search procedure that adds and removes points until a local minima is reached.
source: Following initialization which is based on the expression values, we employ a greedy search procedure that adds and removes points until a local minima is reached (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the TPS algorithm.

claim: Singh et al presented an iterative process which starts with profiling a small number of time points and then selects the next time point based on an Active Learning method.
source: Singh et al (Singh et al., 2005) and Rosa et al (Rosa et al., 2012) presented an iterative process which starts with profiling a small number of time points and then selects the next time point either based on an Active Learning method (Singh et al., 2005) or based on using prior related experiments (Rosa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2005 and Rosa et al., 2012.

claim: Rosa et al presented an iterative process which selects the next time point based on using prior related experiments.
source: Singh et al (Singh et al., 2005) and Rosa et al (Rosa et al., 2012) presented an iterative process which starts with profiling a small number of time points and then selects the next time point either based on an Active Learning method (Singh et al., 2005) or based on using prior related experiments (Rosa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rosa et al., 2012.

claim: Both Singh et al and Rosa et al methods require several iterations until the final time series is profiled, which can drastically lengthen the experiment time and can introduce additional biases.
source: Both of these methods require several iterations until the final time series is profiled, which can drastically lengthen the experiment time and can introduce additional biases making them less useful in practice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the iterative nature of the methods described by Singh et al and Rosa et al.

claim: Normal development of lung alveoli through the process of alveolar septation is a dynamic, coordinated process that requires the accurate spatial and temporal integration of signals.
source: Normal development of lung alveoli through the process of alveolar septation is a dynamic, coordinated process that requires the accurate spatial and temporal integration of signals.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge about lung development.

claim: We currently lack a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic networks that govern normal alveolar septation.
source: We currently lack a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic networks that govern normal alveolar septation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The miRNA data represent an unbiased sample providing information on whether using one type of genomic data can be helpful for determining rates for other types.
source: Thus, the miRNA data represent an unbiased sample providing information on whether using one type of genomic data can be helpful for determining rates for other types.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the miRNA dataset and its utility for testing the TPS method.

claim: Targeted bisulfite sequencing was used to profile three CpG-enriched regions for 13 genes at 8 of the 42 time points.
source: To test the ability of the mRNA data to determine the appropriate points for DNA methylation analysis, we used targeted bisulfite sequencing to profile three CpG-enriched regions for 13 genes at 8 of the 42 time points used for the mRNA and miRNA studies (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methodology for DNA methylation analysis.

claim: In several cases, strong negative or positive correlations were observed between methylation and expression datasets in the time points used.
source: As can be seen, in several cases we observed strong negative or positive correlations between the two datasets in the time points we used serving as another indication for the ability to use one dataset to select the sampling points for the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5, showing correlations between methylation and expression.

claim: TPS is the first non iterative method to address the issue of sampling rates across all different genomic data types.
source: Here, we propose the first non iterative method to address the issue of sampling rates across all different genomic data types.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the TPS method compared to prior work.

claim: A method for selecting time points for these experiments is required to accommodate over a hundred curves (for all genes) simultaneously.
source: Note that unlike standard curve fitting algorithms, a method for selecting time points for these experiments is required to accommodate over a hundred curves (for all genes) simultaneously, and we discuss various ways to formulate this as an optimization problem.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements and challenges of the time point selection problem.

claim: The number of points selected by TPS can either be set in advance by the user or can be defined as a function of the reconstruction error.
source: The number of points selected can either be set in advance by the user (for example, based on budget constraints) or can be defined as a function of the reconstruction error.
evidence: This is a description of the flexibility of the TPS method.

claim: Sorting initial points by absolute values improves the performance highlighting the importance of initialization when searching large combinatorial spaces.
source: Sorting initial points by absolute values further improves the performance highlighting the importance of initialization when searching large combinatorial spaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2, comparing different initialization methods.

claim: Simulated annealing, weighting, and multiple point selection improve performance as well.
source: Simulated annealing, weighting, and multiple point selection improve performance as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2, comparing different search strategies.

claim: Even when using a set where 75% of genes are replaced with random profiles, the time points selected by TPS greatly improve upon an arbitrary set of the same number of time points.
source: As we show in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, even when using such set, the time points selected by TPS greatly improve upon an arbitrary set of the same number of time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In most time series experiments at least 25% of the genes are differentially expressed.
source: Since in most time series experiments at least 25% of the genes are differentially expressed (and in several cases a much larger fraction, (Zhou et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2009 and Shi et al., 2015.

claim: A random selection of genes is likely to exhibit similar results even for poorly understood processes.
source: a random selection of genes is likely to exhibit similar results even for poorly understood processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that at least 25% of genes are typically differentially expressed.

claim: The performance when using the miRNA data itself is better than when using the mRNA data.
source: As expected, the performance when using the miRNA data itself is better than when using the mRNA data.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of errors in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: When taking into account the inherent noise in the data, the differences between using mRNA vs miRNA data for point selection are not large.
source: However, when taking into account the inherent noise in the data the differences are not large.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the reconstruction errors to the noise level in the data.

claim: The points selected by TPS lead to reconstruction errors that are lower than those observed for uniform sampling or for a random set of the same number of points for protein profiling.
source: Specifically, the points selected by TPS lead to reconstruction errors that are lower than those observed for uniform sampling or for a random set of the same number of points further demonstrating the general applicability of our method.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein profiling data discussed in the Appendix Results.

claim: Important expression changes in key genes are missed by using the arbitrary points while the TPS points are able to correctly reconstruct these profiles even though the total number of points is the same.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6, important expression changes in key genes are missed by using the arbitrary points while the TPS points are able to correctly reconstruct these profiles even though the total number of points is the same (5).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual comparison in Figure 6.

claim: The error for the arbitrary set of selected points is much higher on average.
source: More globally, the error for the arbitrary set of selected points is much higher on average (Appendix 2—Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 2—Table 4.

claim: Accurate selection of time points can have a large impact on the ability of the study to identify key genes and events.
source: This indicates that accurate selection of time points can have a large impact on the ability of the study to identify key genes and events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of TPS to prior sampling methods shown in Figure 6.

claim: TPS is implemented in Python and is available on the supporting website.
source: TPS, including all initialization methods discussed, is implemented in Python and is available on the supporting website.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of the TPS software.

claim: The first and last time point can usually be determined by the researcher.
source: In most studies, the first and last time point can usually be determined by the researcher (for example, the time from birth to full lung structural development and maturation in mice).
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in time series experimental design.

claim: The number of samples required between the first and last time points and the sampling frequency are often hard to determine based on phenotypic observations since the molecular events of interest may precede such phenotypic events.
source: However, the number of samples required between these two points and the sampling frequency (given a fixed budget) are often hard to determine based on phenotypic observations since the molecular events of interest may precede such phenotypic events.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in experimental design for time series studies.

claim: Sampling rates have largely been determined using one of two ad-hoc protocols: uniform sampling or nonuniform sampling based on some knowledge of the process.
source: To date, sampling rates have largely been determined using one of two ad-hoc protocols. The first utilized uniform sampling across the duration of the study (Li et al., 2013) with the number of samples constrained by the available budget and samples. The second relied on some (conceived or real) knowledge of the process, often based on phenotypic observations. These studies, especially for responses though also for development, have often used nonuniform sampling (Schulz et al., 2013; Bar-Joseph et al., 2003a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2013, Schulz et al., 2013, and Bar-Joseph et al., 2003a.

claim: It is hard to determine if nonuniform sampling based on phenotypic observations misses important molecular events between the sampled points.
source: though it is hard to determine if such sampling misses important molecular events between the sampled points.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current sampling approaches.

claim: Relatively little work has focused so far on the selection of time points to sample in high throughput time series studies.
source: Relatively, little work has focused so far on the selection of time points to sample in high throughput time series studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: The methods by Singh et al and Rosa et al employ a stopping criteria that does not take into account the full profile.
source: In addition, these methods employ a stopping criteria that does not take into account the full profile and also require that related time series expression experiments be used to select the point, which may be problematic when studying new processes or treatments.
evidence: This is a critique of prior methods based on their design.

claim: The methods by Singh et al and Rosa et al require that related time series expression experiments be used to select the point, which may be problematic when studying new processes or treatments.
source: In addition, these methods employ a stopping criteria that does not take into account the full profile and also require that related time series expression experiments be used to select the point, which may be problematic when studying new processes or treatments.
evidence: This is a critique of prior methods based on their requirements.

claim: For most processes, a small set of genes associated with the process is usually known in advance.
source: Our method starts by selecting a small set of genes that are known to be associated with the process being studied (while the full set is often unknown, for most processes a small set is usually known in advance).
evidence: This is a statement about typical prior knowledge available for biological processes.

claim: The relative ordering of the performance of each of the methods is similar to the mRNA results for miRNA data.
source: More generally, even though the noise in the miRNA data is higher than for the mRNA dataset, relative ordering of the performance of each of the methods is similar to the mRNA results in Figure 2.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparing Figure 2 and Figure 4.

claim: The noise in the miRNA data is higher than for the mRNA dataset.
source: More generally, even though the noise in the miRNA data is higher than for the mRNA dataset, relative ordering of the performance of each of the methods is similar to the mRNA results in Figure 2.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of noise levels between datasets.

claim: mRNAs can serve as a general proxy for selecting time points for other genomic datasets.
source: This serves as a strong indication that mRNAs can serve as a general proxy for selecting time points for other genomic datasets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar performance patterns observed across different data types.

claim: A relatively inexpensive, gene centric, method provides a very good solution for RNA expression profiling as well as other types of data including miRNAs and DNA methylation.
source: As we show, a relatively inexpensive, gene centric, method provides a very good solution for RNA expression profiling as well as other types of data including miRNAs and DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the results presented for multiple data types.

claim: A combined experiment can be fully designed using the TPS method.
source: Thus, a combined experiment can be fully designed using our method.
evidence: This is an inference about the applicability of TPS to experimental design.

claim: TPS has only been tested so far on data for a specific biological process (lung development in mice).
source: While we evaluated TPS on several types of high throughput data, we have only tested it so far on data for a specific biological process (lung development in mice).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: Analysis of additional datasets may identify new challenges that have not been addressed.
source: While we believe that such data is both challenging and representative and thus provides a good test case for the method, analysis of additional datasets may identify new challenges that we have not addressed and we leave it to future work to address these.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future work and limitations.

claim: The lung development data is both challenging and representative and thus provides a good test case for the method.
source: While we believe that such data is both challenging and representative and thus provides a good test case for the method
evidence: This is a claim about the suitability of the test case used in the study.

claim: Certain time points seem to be widely used across studies (for example, 7d) while others were profiled in only one or two of the studies (2d, 10d, three weeks).
source: As can be seen, while certain time points seem to be widely used across studies (for example, 7d) others were profiled in only one or two of the studies (2d, 10d, three weeks).
evidence: This is an observation based on the data presented in Table 1.

claim: It is very hard to compare or combine datasets from different lung development studies due to different time points used.
source: This raises several issues. First, it is very hard to compare or combine these datasets (for example, protein levels were not profiled on day 7(Cox et al., 2007) whereas all mRNA levels were).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of inconsistent time points across studies.

claim: It is hard to determine if differences between DE genes or miRNAs between studies are the result of differences in the underlying conditions studied or simply the result of different sampling.
source: It also makes it hard to determine if differences between DE genes or miRNAs between these studies are the result of differences in the underlying conditions studied (for example, when testing for mutants or treatments) or simply the result of different sampling.
evidence: This is an inference about the challenges in interpreting results from studies with different sampling strategies.

claim: Each of the prior lung development studies may have missed key genes, proteins or miRNAs because of the sampling used.
source: Finally, each of these studies may have missed key genes, proteins or miRNAs because of the sampling used restricting the ability of downstream analysis to use the data to model causal and regulatory events in lung development.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of prior studies.

claim: The sampling used in prior studies restricts the ability of downstream analysis to use the data to model causal and regulatory events in lung development.
source: Finally, each of these studies may have missed key genes, proteins or miRNAs because of the sampling used restricting the ability of downstream analysis to use the data to model causal and regulatory events in lung development.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of sampling strategies on downstream analysis.

claim: Early work on the analysis of cell cycle data in yeast utilized both uniform and nonuniform sampling.
source: For example, early work on the analysis of cell cycle data in yeast utilized both uniform and nonuniform sampling (Spellman et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spellman et al., 1998.

claim: Recent studies of circadian rhythms have followed a similar pattern of using both uniform and nonuniform sampling.
source: and recent studies of circadian rhythms have followed a similar pattern (Storch et al., 2002; Ueda et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Storch et al., 2002 and Ueda et al., 2002.

claim: More recent analysis of responses to flu diverged widely in the (nonuniform) sampling rates that were used.
source: Similarly, more recent analysis of responses to flu diverged widely in the (nonuniform) sampling rates that were used (Shapira et al., 2009; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shapira et al., 2009 and Li et al., 2011.

claim: TPS addresses the problems of inconsistent sampling by using a principled method for determining sampling rates.
source: TPS addresses these problems by using a principled method for determining sampling rates.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of TPS to addressing existing problems in the field.

claim: An important goal in the development of TPS was to enable it to be successfully applied to different types of biological datasets.
source: An important goal in the development of TPS was to enable it to be successfully applied to different types of biological datasets.
evidence: This is a statement about the design goals of the TPS method.
